title: Looking back: year three
hookLine: the great story, the disciples, the roads, the teachers
tomorrow: free yourself first, or stay until everyone is free?

cards: Some of the best advice people ever get comes from someone who says, up front, I'm no expert. Year three told the great story: the life, the disciples, the roads, the teachers. And there's an odd detail in it.
Two seekers, Sariputta and Moggallana, had a pact: whoever finds the deathless first tells the other. One morning Sariputta sees a monk on his alms round, Assaji, so calm it stops him.
Who's your teacher, he asks, and what does he teach? Assaji's answer: I'm new. I've only just gone forth.
I can't teach it at length. A beginner, saying so. That's who brings the Buddha his two chief disciples.

teach.h: ONE SHORT VERSE: THE CAUSE, THE END.
teach.b: So why does the Vinaya hand this turn to a beginner? Look at what Assaji does next. He doesn't refuse, and he doesn't pretend.
He offers what he has, the gist, in one short verse: of things that arise from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause, and also how they end. That's all.

Sariputta hears it, and the text says the clear eye of the teaching opens in him. He runs to Moggallana, who sees at once that something has changed. Sariputta repeats the verse, and the same thing happens again.

teach.h: "THESE TWO WILL BE MY CHIEF PAIR."
teach.b: The two go to the Buddha together, and in the Vinaya the Buddha, seeing them come, says these two will be his chief pair of disciples. Here's the puzzle solved. The teaching didn't need an expert to travel.
It needed someone who had tasted it and passed on the piece he had. A later commentary adds that Sariputta honored Assaji all his life.
That's the great story's quiet engine: not only the Buddha, but the disciples, handing it on, hand to hand.
The great story is still being told that way.

how: Buddhists honor the teachers who passed the dhamma on to them; in temples the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta and Moggallana, are often shown standing on either side of him.

o: comparing your progress to the people around you
turning to a past year of the path to see what it gave
leaving the path to start again from the beginning

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: said 'i'm new' and gave one verse
heard it, then ran to tell his friend
heard it second-hand, and saw too

s: the Buddha's chief disciples were won over by a long debate
it was one short verse, from a monk who said he was new.
Assaji refused to teach because he was a beginner
he said he couldn't teach it at length, then gave the gist anyway.
Moggallana heard the verse from Sariputta, not from Assaji
Sariputta kept the pact and passed it on.

games.q: a coworker asks how you keep steady on deadline days. you've only practiced a little while yourself. what does Assaji's answer suggest?
o: say you're still new, then share the one thing that has helped you.
say nothing until you've practiced for years; beginners mislead.
explain the whole path in detail so you sound like you know it.
games.why: Assaji did both: 'i'm new', then the gist. one honest verse was enough to start the great story's next chapter.

practice: Count the teachers you've had on this path, and not only the well-known ones: a book, a grandparent, a friend who said one sentence at the right time. Touch a finger for each one.
When you run out of names, stay with the last one for the rest of the sit, and let yourself be grateful for the piece they passed on.

wordCard.voice: Looking back, at year three: the great story, and the beginner whose one verse sent the Buddha two great disciples.

orig.note: Pali: cause; the key word in Assaji's verse, about things that arise from a cause.

carryVoice: For the road: the great story, carried by beginners as much as by masters. Three of fourteen.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.23-24 (Sariputta and Moggallana meet Assaji and go to the Buddha)
commentarial tradition (Sariputta's lifelong honor for Assaji)
